grand_strategy.reading: India's grand strategy is relational manoeuvre among the great powers. In Luttwak's terms it is the strategy of a state strong enough to refuse a patron and not strong enough to ignore any of them: it extracts from each - US technology and defence frameworks, Russian oil and arms, Chinese inputs and a quiet border, European markets, Gulf energy and money, Japanese capital - by being too large to coerce and too useful to lose. The paradoxical logic is that each of these relations is also a pressure point, and the pressures are not independent. The week of 11-17 September 2026 shows the shape: Putin in Delhi on the 11th, Xi on the 12th, the US Congress passing a tariff authority on Russian oil buyers on the 17th. The culminating point of manoeuvre is reached when all three pull at once and the price of waiting - a tariff, a border incident, a sanction - overtakes the benefit of keeping options open; in July, with the Hormuz war on, Russian imports hit 2.8 million barrels a day just when Washington sought less of them, and the US-India trade agreement that would reward a shift remains unsigned. The Pakistan file is read here as rivalry, not mortal enmity: New Delhi's declared aim is deterrence of terrorism, with a reversible lever (the Indus treaty) and an accepted ceasefire, and it does not seek the end of the Pakistani state - which is what separates it from Israel and Iran. The neighbourhood is where the strategy is least comfortable: the instruments of primacy (credit lines, hydropower, refuge for Hasina) generate reactions that open space for China. Confidence in this reading is moderate: it rests on tier-3 press for most 2026 events, and several figures (Indonesian and Vietnamese BrahMos values, the Rafale and submarine contracts, the status of the US sanctions act) are unconfirmed.

stances.note: The ontology's adversary test: does New Delhi seek the end of the Pakistani state or its regime? The record says no. After the Pahalgam attack (22 Apr 2025, 26 killed, claimed by TRF, which India calls a Lashkar-e-Taiba front) India struck nine 'terrorist sites' in Operation Sindoor on 7 May 2025, fought four days of missile, drone and artillery exchanges, and then accepted a ceasefire agreed between the two DGMOs on 10 May; it targets terror infrastructure and the army's sponsorship of it, calls the new line 'if Pakistan fires, we fire', and keeps the Pakistani state as the counterpart it holds responsible. The Indus Waters Treaty is 'in abeyance' since 23 Apr 2025 'until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures cross-border terrorism' (MEA, 3 Jul 2026) - leverage with a stated exit condition, not an end-state. India does claim all of Jammu and Kashmir including Pakistan-held territory, and engagement is now limited to terrorism and PoK. After the Red Fort car bomb in Delhi (10 Nov 2025, 12-15 killed, a Jaish-e-Mohammed link noted by the UN monitoring team in Feb 2026) India did not formally blame Pakistan or retaliate, which shows the threshold is attribution, not each incident. That is a rivalry with a nuclear shadow and an arms race, not a war of existence, so `rival`, not `adversary`; the Pakistani side (Munir's army, the Saudi pact, Chinese kit) reads India as the existential threat, which is why the pair is asymmetric in feeling but not in grade. Mediation is refused (Kashmir is bilateral; India denies the US brokered the ceasefire). Bond - grievance: partition, four wars, Kashmir. Confidence B because the grade is our structural reading of sources that describe the pair as rivals and India's own posture as deterrence.

stances.note: A partner whose year was a stress test. The 2025 US tariffs reached 50% in Aug 2025 (25% 'reciprocal' plus 25% for buying Russian oil) and put ties 'at their lowest in nearly two decades' (Tribune); the 100,000-dollar H-1B fee (19 Sep 2025) hit the pipeline of Indian engineers (Indians were 71% of 2024 approvals). Repair followed: the 10-year Framework for the US-India Major Defence Partnership signed in Kuala Lumpur on 31 Oct 2025, the 2 Feb 2026 deal cutting the rate to 18% in exchange for restricting Russian oil and buying more American goods, the Quad foreign ministers in New Delhi on 26 May 2026. But the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 20 Feb 2026, the first-phase trade agreement is still unsigned (Goyal in June: '99 percent' settled), the Quad leaders' summit India was to host has no date, and on 17 Sep 2026 Congress passed an act authorising tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, to which the MEA answered it will 'take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests'. Net direction: neither warming nor cooling, with the US pulling harder on Russian oil than at any time since 2022. Not an ally: no treaty, no basing, India refuses mediation on Pakistan and keeps Russia. Bond - affinity: diaspora, technology, shared China concern.
